paragraphs: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi.

Hyman writes: His father, Rav Idi, was called Rav Idi bar Avin, and it is related in Pesachim 49a that he married a priest's daughter, "and two ordained sons [סמיכי] came forth from him, Rav Shisha and Rav Yehoshua." His father, Rav Idi bar Avin, lived in the time of Rava and Rav Pappa, as explained in his entry, and his son Rav Yehoshua was the leading figure of the generation in the time of Rav Ashi. As in Shabbat 11a: when he happened to come to Rav Ashi's house, they prepared a calf (igla tilta) for him; he said to him, "Will the master taste something?" — He said to him, "I am sitting in a fast on account of a dream." Hyman adds that in Taanit 12b the reading is that he came to the house of Rav Asi, and it should read Rav Ashi, or else it is Rav Asi who was the colleague of Rav Ashi, as explained in his entry. And in Yevamot 36b Rav Ashi challenged him, "Is this comparable?" And he is mentioned in halakhah in Eruvin 82b and Moed Katan 5.

And he was present at the death of Rav Kahana, as in Pesachim 3b: When Rav Kahana fell ill, the Rabbis sent Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi (the father’s name is abbreviated ר״א here), saying, "Go and check." He found that he had died; he tore his garment — and wept and came back. They said to him, "Did he die?" He said, "I did not say so, and one who spreads slander..." etc. Hyman continues: Yuchasin cites R' Yehoshua bar Idi bar Avin the carpenter, but the truth is not so, for R' Avin the carpenter was in the days of Rav Huna, as in Shabbat 23b,

Hyman continues: His son Rav Idi was a student of Rav Chisda, as in Pesachim 101b. If so, how could Rav Yehoshua his son be alive in the days of Rav Ashi? It is plausible that he was a grandson of the well-known Ravin.

notes.text: Hyman writes Rav Shisha; the named Davidson Pesachim49a has Rav Sheshet. Semikhi describes the two sons’ scholarly standing, not physical adjacency. Pesachim3b explicitly makes the rabbis ask whether Kahana has died; he does not speak after death.

The named Shabbat23b explicitly has Rav Huna before Avin the carpenter. Hyman’s chronology, Ashi/Asi alternatives and proposed grandson-of-Ravin connection remain his arguments. The exact calf term igla tilta still needs its explanatory context.

The saved William Davidson Pesachim 49a paragraph reads Rav Sheshet beside Rabbi Yehoshua, whereas Hyman supplies Rav Shisha and Rav Yehoshua. His names and explicit Rav titles remain unchanged. The named English translation describes the two semikhi sons as ordained to decide halakhic matters; ordained here follows that local lexical explanation and does not newly establish an ordination history. Pesachim 3b makes the rabbis ask whether Rav Kahana has died, and Shabbat 23b explicitly names Rav Huna and Rabbi Avin the carpenter. The supplied abbreviation ר״א remains visible without a Hebrew repair. The Yuchasin-related titles in the new body retain Hyman’s R' abbreviation, without transferring a fuller title from another occurrence. Hyman’s leading-figure chronology, Ashi/Asi correction or alternative, emphatic rejection of the Yuchasin identification, genuine chronological question and tentative grandson-of-Ravin suggestion remain his claims, without a new genealogy or teacher identity admission. No new Shabbat 11a, Taanit 12b, Yevamot 36b, Eruvin 82b, Moed Katan 5 or Pesachim 101b passage has been collated for this change; the calf term and p002 source hold remain unresolved. Both existing mixed notes remain verbatim. No further laws, figures or details from the selected digital paragraphs are imported, and no printed-pixel or correction-history verification is claimed.

The printed notice spans volume II, pages 620–621. In addition to the earlier comparisons recorded above, the whole named Shabbat 11a paragraph has Rav Ashi, whereas Taanit 12b has Rav Assi; both use plural speakers when inviting the visitor to eat. Hyman’s abbreviated quotation does not name that speaker, so the English no longer inserts Rav Ashi as the questioner. Davidson’s Taanit translation explains igla tilta as a third-born calf; the body preserves the Aramaic term without adding that explanation to Hyman’s quotation. Hyman’s correction to Ashi, alternative identification with Ashi’s colleague, leading-generation chronology, emphatic rejection of the Yuchasin genealogy and tentative grandson-of-Ravin suggestion remain his own arguments at their original strength. The exact Yuchasin printing has not been collated. Pesachim 49a reads Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yehoshua beside Hyman’s Rav Shisha and Rav Yehoshua; these supplied names are retained. No identification of the different Asi or Idi notices follows from these comparisons.
